params.place: on the map: the Panama Canal across the isthmus, the lake in its middle

moments.what: a rain cloud over the lake thins out
Panama's border traces and its flag fills it
the canal line glows from sea to sea
a ship in the canal halts and a STOP sign stamps beside it

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: Without rain, the Panama Canal stops.

params.place: on the map: close over Gatun Lake

moments.what: a question mark drops over the lake
the last raindrops stop
the camera pushes in on the lake
the lake's edge flickers

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: So what if it never rained there again?

params.place: on the map: the canal's Atlantic entrance at Colon, a board of ships a day

moments.what: a sun blazes over the lake
the lake's blue pales and the land browns
a board at the entrance shows ships a day
ships line up at the entrance
the board's figure starts to drop
the board lands on the lower figure and half the ships stop

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: It nearly happened. In a drought, the canal cut the ships crossing each day from 36 to just 22.

params.place: on the map: the canal from Colon over Gatun Lake to Panama City

moments.what: a raindrop icon pulses over the lake
a straight flat ditch draws across and is crossed out
both seas glow at the ends
a ship rises up the steps at the Atlantic end
the lake glows blue
the ship sails across the lake
GATUN LAKE writes over it
the ship steps down at the Pacific end
it reaches the Pacific and PACIFIC writes on the sea

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: Why would a canal need rain? It isn't a flat ditch from sea to sea. Ships climb up into a lake in the middle of Panama, Gatun Lake, then step back down to the other ocean.

place: on the map: close on the Gatun locks at the Caribbean end
on the map: close on the Pacific locks

moments.what: the lake shimmers
ships pass the locks one after another
the first ship goes through the lock
a wave of blue gushes out of the lock
the gush pours into the sea
the lake's edge pulls back a little
streams run out at the other end too
the sea at both ends swells with lake water

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: And where does the water go? Every ship that crosses lets a huge gulp of the lake's fresh water run out into the sea.

params.place: on the map: the rainforest hills round Gatun Lake

moments.what: the camera pulls back over the hills
rivers draw into the lake
clouds roll in and rain falls
the lake grows back
trees pop up round the lake
the forest rings the lake

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: The only thing that fills it back up is rain, falling on the forest all around it.

params.place: on the map: Gatun Lake shrinking, the canal running dry

moments.what: the clouds vanish and the sun comes out
the trees turn brown
the lake shrinks one step
it shrinks again as each ship passes
the lock marks turn red
dry mud cracks open at the lake's edge
the ships on the canal thin out
the last ship crawls across

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: So if the rain stops for good, the lake sinks a little with every ship, the locks run short, and fewer and fewer ships get through.

params.place: on the map: the anchorages off Colon and Panama City

moments.what: the camera rises to show both ends
the two ends flash
ships anchor off each end
more ships join both lines
the lines stretch out to sea
a day counter ticks up over the queues
the ships' containers glow
dotted lines run from the queues off to the edges of the map

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: At both ends, the line of waiting ships grows longer every day, each one loaded with cargo that someone, somewhere, is waiting for.

params.place: on the map: the whole of South America, the route round Cape Horn

moments.what: the camera pulls back from Panama
South America fills the map
a ship sets off east along the coast
the route draws down the Atlantic coast
SOUTH AMERICA writes across it
storm clouds swirl at the tip
the ship rounds the tip
CAPE HORN labels it
the route climbs the Pacific coast
the route reaches Panama again
a calendar over the route flips through weeks
the short canal pulses
the short canal glows at the top of the map

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: Until the only way left is the long way round: all the way down South America, round stormy Cape Horn, and back up the other side. Weeks at sea, instead of about half a day going straight through the canal.

params.place: on the map: the Caribbean and the Pacific, the world's routes meeting at the canal

moments.what: the canal pulses
the share sign starts to rise
shipping routes light up toward Panama
container ships ride the routes
the routes meet at the canal
a sign at the canal shows the share of world sea trade
a car carrier sails in
a grain ship sails in
a tanker sails in
a rain cloud rolls over the canal
rain falls on the lake and the canal glows

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: And about 5% of all the world's trade by sea goes through this one canal: cars, grain and fuel. All of it riding on the rain.

params.place: on the map: back over the Panama Canal

moments.what: a rain cloud pops on the left
a container ship pops on the right
both glow over Panama
a comment bubble pops between them
the camera pulls back over the canal
the cloud thins over the lake

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: Rain or ships: which does Panama need more? Tell me. Because without rain,
